readings.c1s1:
¶
'''amass''' (a̤-mȧs′), ''v. t.'' [< F. ''amasser'', < ML. ''amassare'', < L. ''ad'', to, + ''massa'', mass, heap, > F. ''masse'', > E. ''mass''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.] To collect into a mass or heap; bring together a great amount, quantity, or number of: as, to ''amass'' a fortune.
{{smaller block|In his youth Comte was an insatiable reader, and before he began the work of constructing the Positive Philosophy he had ''amassed'' vast stores of learning in almost every department of knowledge.
{{right|''J. Fiske'', Cos. Phil., I. 136.}}}}

'''amass†''' (a̤-mȧs′), ''n.'' [< OF. ''amasse'', F. ''amas''; from the verb.] An assemblage, a heap, or an accumulation.
{{smaller block|This pillar is nothing in effect but a medley or an ''amasse'' of all the precedent ornaments. {{right|''Wotton'', Reliquiæ, p. 25.}}}}

'''amassable''' (a̤-mȧs′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''amass'' + ''-able.''] Capable of being amassed.

'''amasser''' (a̤-mȧs′ėr), ''n.'' One who amasses or accumulates.

'''amassette''' (am-a̤-set′), ''n.'' [F. (dim. form), < ''amasser'', amass, collect: see ''amass'', ''v.''] An instrument, usually of horn, like a palette-knife or spatula, with which in the preparation of pigments the colors used in painting are collected and scraped together on the stone during the process of grinding them with the muller. Also written ''amazette.''

'''amassment''' (a̤-mȧs′ment), ''n.'' The act of amassing; a heap collected; a great quantity or number brought together; an accumulation.
{{smaller block|An ''amassment'' of imaginary conceptions.
{{right|''Glanville'', Scep. Sci., xiii.}}}}

'''Amasta''' (a-mas′tä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., neut. pl. of ''amastus'', < Gr. ἄμαστος, without breasts, < ἀ-
readings.c1s2:
priv. + μαστός, breast.] Nippleless mammals: a term applied to the monotremes or cloacal oviparous mammals, which, though provided with mammary glands, have no nipples.

'''amasthenic''' (am-as-then′ik), ''a.'' [Prop. *''hamasthenic'', < Gr. ἅμα, together, + σθένος, strength.] Uniting the chemical rays of light in a focus: said of a lens. Also ''amacratic.''

'''amate<sup>1</sup>†''' (a̤-māt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''a-'' (expletive) + ''mate''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] To accompany; entertain as a companion; be a fellow or mate to.
{{smaller block|<poem>A lovely bevy of faire Ladies sate,
Courted of many a jolly Paramoure,
The which them did in modest wise ''amate.''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 34.}}}}

'''amate<sup>2</sup>†''' (a̤-māt′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''amaten'', < OF. ''amatir'', daunt, subdue, enfeeble, etc. (= It. ''ammattire''), < ''a-'' (L. ''ad'', to) + ''matir'', ''mater'' (in same senses as ''amatir''), > E. ''mate'', enfeeble: see ''mate''<sup>2</sup>.] To terrify; perplex; daunt; subdue.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon the wall the Pagans old and young
Stood hush’d and still, ''amated'' and amaz’d.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', tr. of Tasso, xi. 12.}}
<poem>My lord, hath love ''amated'' him whose thoughts
Have ever been heroical and brave?</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Orlando Furioso.}}}}

'''amaterialistic''' (a-ma-tē″ri-a-lis′tik), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀ- priv. (''a-''<sup>18</sup>) + ''materialistic.''] Opposed to materialism, or to materialistic philosophy.
{{smaller block|It is intensely ''amaterialistic'' for us to speak of the table (that is, of any table) as if it had some objective existence, independent of a cognizing mind.
{{right|''J. Fiske'', in N. A. Rev., CXXVI. 33.}}}}

'''amateur''' (am′a̤-tūr or am-a̤-tūr′, often as F., the word being of recent introduction—about
readings.c1s3:
1784 — am-a-tėr′), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [F., = Pr. ''amatour'' = Sp. Pg. ''amador'' = It. ''amatore'', a lover, an amateur, < L. ''amatorem'', acc. of ''amator'', lover, < ''amare'', pp. ''amatus'', love: see ''amor''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who admires; an admirer; a lover.
{{smaller block|She remained an impassioned ''amateur'' of musical genius in others.
{{right|''Howells'', A Modern Instance.}}}}
'''2.''' One who has an especial love for any art, study, or pursuit, but does not practise it.—'''3.''' Most commonly, one who cultivates any study or art from taste or attachment, without pursuing it professionally or with a view to gain: often used of one who pursues a study or an art in a desultory, unskilful, or non-professional way.—'''4.''' Specifically, in ''sporting'' and ''athletics'', an athlete who has never competed in a match open to all comers, or for a stake, or for public money, or for gate-money, or under a false name, or with a professional for a prize, and has never taught or pursued athletic exercises as a means of support.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or having the character of an amateur: as, ''amateur'' work; an ''amateur'' pianist.

'''amateurish''' (am-a-tūr′ish or am-a-tėr′ish), ''a.'' [< ''amateur'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Pertaining to or characteristic of an amateur; having the faults or deficiencies of an amateur or a non-professional.
{{smaller block|A condescending, ''amateurish'' way.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend}}}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
{{smaller block|A small quantity of passion, dexterously meted out, may be ample to inspire an ''amatorial'' poet.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., I. 356.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Amatorial muscles''', the oblique muscles of the eye: so called from their fancied importance in ogling.}}

'''amatorially''' (am-a̤-tō′ri-al-i), ''adv.'' In an amatorial manner; by way of love.

'''amatorian''' (am-a̤-tō′ri-an), ''a.'' Pertaining to love; amatorial. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Horace’s lusory or ''amatorian'' odes.
{{right|''Johnson'', Lives of Poets (Edmund Smith).}}}}

'''amatorio''' (ä-mä-tō′ri-ō), ''n.''; pl. ''amatorii'' (-ē). [It., < L. ''amatorius'': see ''amatory''.] A decorated vase, dish, bowl, or plate, intended or suitable for a love-gift; specifically, a piece of majolica painted with the portrait of a lady and bearing a complimentary inscription.

'''amatorious†''' (am-a̤-tō′ri-us), ''a.'' [< L. ''amatorius'': see ''amatory''.] Pertaining to love.
{{smaller block|The vain, ''amatorious'' poem of Sir Philip Sidney’s “Arcadia.”
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes.}}}}

'''amatory''' (am′a̤-tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''amatorius'', pertaining to love or a lover, < ''amator'', a lover: see ''amateur''. Cf. ''amorous''.] Pertaining to, producing, or supposed to produce love; expressive of love; amatorial: as, ''amatory'' poems.
{{smaller block|<poem>She could repay each ''amatory'' look you lent
With interest.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, ix. 62.}}}}
='''Syn.''' See ''amorous''.

'''amaurosis''' (am-â-rō′sis), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀμαύρωσις, < ἀμαυρός, dim, dark, < ἀ- intensive + μαυρός,
readings.c2s3:
dark.] A partial or total loss of sight independent of any discoverable lesion in the eye itself: formerly and still sometimes called ''gutta serena;'' by Milton “a drop serene,” P. L., iii. 25.

'''amaurotic''' (am-â-rot′ik), ''a.'' Pertaining to or affected with amaurosis.

'''amausite''' (a-mâ′sīt), ''n.'' Same as ''petrosilex.''

'''amay†''' (a-mā′), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' [< ME. ''amayen,'' < OF. ''amaier, amaer,'' forms parallel to the usual OF. ''esmaier, esmaer'' = Pr. ''esmaiar'' = It. ''smagare,'' < L. ''ex,'' out (here privative), + ML. *''magare,'' < OHG. ''magan,'' have power, = E. ''may,'' ''v.'' Cf. ''dismay.''] To dismay; confound; be dismayed.
{{smaller block|Whereof he dradde and was ''amayed.''
{{right|''Gower,'' Conf. Amant.}}}}
{{smaller block|Counsayllen the of that thou art ''amayed.''
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Troilus, i. 648.}}}}

'''amaze''' (a̤-māz′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''amazed,'' ppr. ''amazing.'' [< ME. ''amasen,'' found only in pp. ''amased;'' also ''bimased,'' in same sense; < ''a-,'' E. ''a-''<sup>1</sup> (or ''bi-,'' E. ''be-''<sup>1</sup>), + ''masen,'' confuse, perplex, > E. ''maze,'' q. v.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder; confuse; perplex.
{{smaller block|They shall be afraid; . . . they shall be ''amazed'' one at another.
{{right|Isa. xiii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let thy blows, doubly redoubled,
Fall like ''amazing'' thunder on the casque
Of thy adverse pernicious enemy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Rich. II., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Till the great plover’s human whistle ''amazed''
Her heart, and glancing round the waste she fear’d
In every wavering brake an ambuscade.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson,'' Geraint.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|The beauty and magnificence of the buildings erected by the sovereigns of Hindostan ''amazed'' even travellers who had seen St. Peter’s. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Clive.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then down into the vale he gazed,
And held his breath, as if ''amazed''
By all its wondrous loveliness.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 104.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Surprise, Astonish'', etc. (see ''surprise''); to confound, stagger, stupefy, dumfound.

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To wonder; be amazed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Madam, ''amaze'' not; see his majesty
Return’d with glory from the Holy Land.</poem>
{{right|''Peele'', Edward I., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Amaze'' not, man of God, if in the spirit
Thou’rt brought from Jewry unto Nineveh.</poem>
{{right|''Greene and Lodge'', Look. Glass for L. and E., p. 119.}}}}

'''amaze''' (a̤-māz′), ''n.'' [< ''amaze'', ''v.''] Astonishment; confusion; perplexity arising from fear, surprise, or wonder; amazement: used chiefly in poetry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Now of my own accord such other trial
I mean to show you of my strength, yet greater,
As with ''amaze'' shall strike all who behold.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1645.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It fills me with ''amaze''
To see thee, Porphyro!</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Eve of St, Agnes.}}}}

'''amazedly''' (a̤-mā′zed-li), ''adv.'' With amazement; in a manner that indicates astonishment or bewilderment.
readings.c3s2:
¶
{{smaller block|<poem>I speak ''amazedly''; and it becomes
My marvel, and my message.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 1.}}}}

'''amazedness''' (a̤-mā′zed-nes), ''n.'' The state of being amazed or confounded with fear, surprise, or wonder; astonishment; great wonder.
{{smaller block|After a little ''amazedness'', we were all commanded out of the chamber.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 2.}}}}

'''amazeful†''' (a̤-māz′fu̇l), ''a.'' Full of amazement; calculated to produce amazement.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy just armes
Shine with ''amazefull'' terror.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Sophonisba, i. 1.}}}}

'''amazement''' (a̤-māz′ment), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state of being amazed; astonishment; confusion or perplexity from a sudden impression of surprise, or surprise mingled with alarm.
{{smaller block|They were filled with wonder and ''amazement'' at that which had happened unto him.
{{right|Acts iii. 10.}}
<poem>His words impression left
Of much ''amazement'' to the infernal crew.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., i. 107.}}}}
'''2†.''' Infatuation; madness. ''Webster.''

'''amazette''' (am-a̤-zet′), ''n.'' Same as ''amassette.''

'''Amazilia''' (am-a̤-zil′i-ä), ''n.'' [NL., < ''amazili'', applied by the French ornithologist Lesson in 1826 to a species of humming-bird, and in 1832, in pl., to a group of humming-birds. Other NL. forms are ''amazilius, amazilicus, amazillis, amazillia, amizilis'' (a mere misprint), dim. ''amazicula, amaziliculus:'' all being names of humming-birds. The name ''amazili'' is prob. of S. Amer. origin, perhaps connected with the name of the ''Amazon'' river; cf. ''amazon''<sup>2</sup>, 2.] A genus

The name ''amazili'' is prob. of S. Amer. origin, perhaps connected with the name of the ''Amazon'' river; cf. ''amazon''2, 2.]   A genus of humming-birds, of the family ''Trochilidæ'', embracing about 24 species, of large size, found from the Mexican border of the United States to Peru, and mostly of green and chestnut coloration. {{smaller|The bill is about as long as the head, nearly straight, and broad, with lancet-shaped tip; the nostrils are exposed and scaled; the wings are long and pointed; the tail is even or slightly forked; and the tarsi are feathered.
